title: Diego Garcia
description: Atoll in the Chagos Archipelago, Indian Ocean
wiki_lead:
Diego Garcia () is a coral atoll in the central Indian Ocean, the largest and southernmost of the atolls of the Chagos Archipelago. Its nearly continuous, V-shaped rim of land, about 64 kilometres (40 mi) long, almost encloses a lagoon of 124 square kilometres (48 sq mi) and holds more than half of the archipelago's land. Administered by the United Kingdom as part of the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT), and claimed by Mauritius, it is the site of a joint British–American military base, Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia; it has no permanent inhabitants, and around 2,000 military personnel, officials and contractors are ordinarily present.
Known to Portuguese navigators from the early 16th century and claimed by France from 1769, the atoll was settled from the 1780s by planters from Île de France (Mauritius) with enslaved workers brought mainly from Madagascar and Mozambique. It passed to Britain with Mauritius in 1810–1814, and for 150 years its plantations at East Point, Pointe Marianne and Minni Minni produced coconut oil and copra; it was briefly a coaling station in the 1880s and a flying-boat base in the Second World War. The descendants of the plantation workers formed a community known as the Ilois, now generally called Chagossians.
In 1965 the United Kingdom detached the archipelago from Mauritius to form the BIOT and, under the 1966 UK–US exchange of notes, made it available for the defence purposes of both governments. The inhabitants of Diego Garcia were removed in 1971, and the rest of the archipelago was emptied by 1973 (see Expulsion of the Chagossians). An American naval communications station built from 1971 was expanded under the Diego Garcia Agreement 1976 into a naval support facility, which has since been used for operations in the Gulf, Iraq and Afghanistan; in 2008 the British government acknowledged that the island had been used for two American extraordinary rendition flights in 2002.
The atoll is at the centre of the Chagos Archipelago sovereignty dispute: in 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that the United Kingdom should end its administration of the archipelago "as rapidly as possible". Under the treaty signed on 22 May 2025, the United Kingdom would accept that "Mauritius is sovereign over the Chagos Archipelago in its entirety, including Diego Garcia", and Mauritius would authorise it to exercise sovereign rights over Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years. After the position of the US president, Donald Trump, changed in 2026, the British government said that it could not ratify the treaty without American support, and as of November 2026 it had not entered into force. In March 2026, during the war between the United States, Israel and Iran, two Iranian ballistic missiles were launched towards the island; according to the British Defence Secretary, neither got close to it.

grok_lead: Diego Garcia is a V-shaped coral atoll and the largest island in the Chagos Archipelago, located in the central Indian Ocean at approximately 7Â°S latitude and 72Â°E longitude, forming the principal landmass of the British Indian Ocean Territory. The atoll, spanning about 44 square kilometers with a lagoon nearly 19 kilometers long, hosts Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia, a joint United KingdomâUnited States military installation established in the 1970s following the 1966 bilateral exchange of notes that authorized its development for strategic logistics and support roles. Its remote position enables prepositioning of materiel, aerial refueling, and sustainment for operations across the Indian Ocean region and beyond, serving as a critical node for U.S. Central, European, Africa, and Indo-Pacific combatant commands without direct exposure to littoral threats. The base's construction necessitated the closure of copra plantations and the compulsory relocation of roughly 1,500â2,000 Chagossian inhabitants from the Chagos islands to Mauritius and the Seychelles between 1968 and 1973, a process tied to securing the site for unrestricted military use. In 2024, the UK reached an agreement with Mauritius to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago, including Diego Garcia, while preserving the base's operations through a 99-year leasing arrangement with the United States, though the deal has faced objections from U.S. President Donald Trump in January 2026, leading to reopened discussions and potential risks to its implementation. On March 20, 2026, Iran launched two ballistic missiles targeting the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia. The attack was unsuccessful: one missile failed mid-flight and a U.S. destroyer launched SM-3 interceptors at the second, though it could not be determined if an interception occurred; neither reached the target or caused damage, demonstrating Iran's extended missile range capabilities. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated the alliance could not confirm Israel's claim of Iranian involvement or intercontinental capabilities, but emphasized assessing Iran's missile threat and supporting US responses. Iran denied responsibility, with a senior official stating to Al Jazeera that Tehran was not behind the strikes. The UK foreign secretary condemned Iran's actions as "reckless threats" and the government agreed to allow US forces to use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for limited defensive operations targeting Iranian missile sites.
